item.text: {"winner":"B","confidence":"high","summary":"B follows the frozen API design directly and with substantially less behavioral churn. A improves retry coverage but violates explicit contract boundaries by changing Add and bypassing it from Upload.","reasons":["B preserves FilesService.Add unchanged, while A makes Add eagerly consume and buffer every caller-provided body, changing streaming, memory, timing, and reader-error behavior.","B routes the multipart body through s.Add exactly as required; A introduces a private add path and calls that directly from Upload.","B explicitly validates both an empty filename and nil content before encoding or requesting.","Both reuse internal/multipartbody.NewFile and preserve FilesOption forwarding, but B does so with simpler, established composition rather than splitting Add's implementation across two methods."],"risks_a":["Changing Add to io.ReadAll is outside the requested scope and can impose unbounded memory use on the lower-level custom-body API.","Upload bypasses Add, contrary to the contract's requirement to keep request construction, option handling, decoding, and errors centralized there.","Upload has no visible service-level validation and relies on multipartbody.NewFile for the required empty-name and nil-reader checks, while its tests do not cover those cases or source-reader failures."],"risks_b":["The retry test counts requests but does not read and compare the multipart body on both attempts, so it would not detect an empty replayed body.","The retry test uses strings.NewReader rather than an os.File or other streamed source and does not set RetryAllMethods, making it less representative of the reported scenario.","Tests do not cover validation or propagation of source-reader errors, and the exported Upload method lacks a Go documentation comment."]}
